title: An audit scoped to five items reported "no divergences"

validator.title: An audit scoped to five items reported "no divergences"
validator.root_cause: Confirmed by inspection: DEVLOG Entry 020 (2026-03-14) records that the 5-item audit reported 'no divergences' and missed IsDivisionKeyword vs IsDivisionStart (a bug in 32 NIST programs); the full every-production audit then found 80 issues. Under-scoping, not a missing capability, produced the false confidence.
validator.evidence: Entry 020: 'The full audit found 80 issues - 7 critical, 20 medium, 30 low. A full day was wasted between the incomplete audit and the comprehensive one.' 32 NIST programs matches. Figures match the candidate.
validator.battle_tested: The denominator fix has been in continuous use since: the rule catalog / traceability inventory (4,348 rows, GAP as the progress metric) drives every later wave (e.g. DEVLOG line 6431: 'GAP 2407 -> 2396, denominator unchanged at 4,348'). Measured effect: Entry 1424 (2026-09-01) used the denominator to show 92% of the GAP (3,361 of 3,636 rows) had never been adjudicated while review fleets polished 27 rows, and redirected the campaign. The 'completeness critic' half of the fix (review skill Scale) has no recorded exercise; the catalog-denominator half carries the verdict.
validator.correction: The 'completeness critic' in the review skill's Scale section is unexercised in the record; the battle-tested fix is the rule-catalog denominator.

title: Find-then-verify reviews find real bugs in every phase; verify by running

validator.title: Find-then-verify reviews find real bugs in every phase; verify by running
validator.root_cause: Established by measurement: Entry 603 (2026-07-04). All 9 oo_* goldens were green on the first build, yet the find->verify workflow confirmed 22 real conformance bugs by running probe programs (e.g. slice 2's 'strict 14.8.2 conformance everywhere' misread the spec). The happy-path tests the author wrote did not reach them.
validator.evidence: Entry 603: '45 agents (4 review lenses ...) -> 29 findings -> 24 adversarially verified -> 22 CONFIRMED / 2 refuted', '3.18M subagent tokens, 858 tool uses, ~23 min wall'. The 'sometimes WRONG in their specifics ... but named REAL bugs' quote is at DEVLOG line 43120 (OCCURS DYNAMIC wave). The candidate omits the 24-verified step; otherwise it matches.
validator.battle_tested: Used across many later waves with confirmed catches each time: Entry 620 (9 real findings), a 25-agent pass that found 3 blockers in a fix (line 28795), and the 2026-08-29..31 fleets of 58, 73, 78, 100 and 106 agents with 14-26 confirmed findings each (lines 16319-16624, 14237). No entry reverses the find-then-verify method.
validator.correction: The chain was 45 agents -> 29 findings -> 24 verified -> 22 confirmed / 2 refuted. Qualifier: Entry 1424 measured that thirteen large review fleets (2026-08-29..31, ~1,000 agents, ~4B cache-read tokens) moved the GAP only 27 rows, so large fleets were de-prioritised in favour of lanes. The method finds real bugs but is costly per row closed.

refuter.title: Find-then-verify reviews find real bugs in every phase; verify by running
refuter.reason: Primary sources contradict the universal claim 'in every phase', and also the validator's 'confirmed catches each time'. Entry 397 (l.51133): a 2-lens, 17-agent adversarial review returned 0 confirmed and 15 refuted. The lander's find-then-verify review of the train diff found 0 confirmed findings in Entry 1721 (l.1467), Entry 1722 (l.1365) and Entry 1743 (l.800). Entry 603 itself records that the 3a/3b surface was solid (12/12 behavior probes); the bugs were elsewhere in the OO wave. What does check out: Entry 603's chain (45 agents -> 29 findings -> 24 adversarially verified -> 22 CONFIRMED / 2 refuted; 3.18M tokens; ~23 min) and the 'sometimes WRONG in their specifics ... but named REAL bugs' quote (l.43120, Entry 657). A narrowed restatement would likely vet and could be resubmitted as a new candidate: find-then-verify reviews repeatedly found real bugs that green goldens missed, a null result is a legitimate outcome, and each finding should be verified by running it. The cost qualifier from Entry 1424 still applies.

title: A registrar re-measures every lead before filing it

validator.title: A registrar re-measures every lead before filing it
validator.root_cause: Established by measurement. Registrar passes that rebuilt and re-ran every probe repeatedly found forwarded leads that were already fixed, mis-scoped or miscited (Entries 1616, 1623, 1633, 1636).
validator.evidence: Entry 1623 (registrar #7): 'THREE REPORTED FINDINGS DID NOT SURVIVE THE RE-RUN', and a quoted 13.18.45.4 GR2 citation was a paraphrase. Entry 1633 (registrar #9): 'a registrar that copies a report's measurement forward is a second place for the report's mistakes to live' is verbatim. Entry 1616: 52 leads, three died. Entry 1636: four leads dropped with the reason.
validator.battle_tested: Sustained across registrars #6, #7, #9, #10, #11 and 14f (2026-09-19..24), each recording dropped or corrected leads. The registrar is a defined role (MANDATORY-PRACTICES R1-R3, templates/registrar-brief.md).
validator.correction: The 'two of four' leads in Entry 1633 were real defects that each carried a wrong claim (a spurious screen-grammar sweep; a misquoted 15.3 rule), not wholly wrong leads. The practice was narrowed on 2026-09-23 (Entry 1664, MANDATORY-PRACTICES R2, reason 'Triple probing'): write a fresh probe on your own build only when the lead lacks a runnable repro and code site; otherwise run the given repro once and record the result. 'Rebuilds, re-runs every probe' overstates the current rule, and the role already exists, so 'not yet as a role' is wrong.

refuter.title: A registrar re-measures every lead before filing it
refuter.reason: (1)(2) Established by measurement across registrar passes. Entry 1616 (l.6549): 52 leads; 'three leads DIED on re-measurement', one of them already fixed. Entry 1623 (l.6039-6045): 'forty-eight' leads; 'THREE REPORTED FINDINGS DID NOT SURVIVE THE RE-RUN'; the 13.18.45.4 GR2 quote was a paraphrase. Entry 1633 (l.5215-5221): the 'second place for the report's mistakes to live' quote is verbatim, and the two leads were REAL defects that carried wrong claims, repeated verbatim by the lander. Entry 1636: four leads dropped with the reason. (3) Narrowed, not reversed. R2 (commit ed699e767, 2026-09-23, 'Triple probing') limits FRESH re-probes to leads with no runnable repro and code site; otherwise the registrar runs the given repro once. (4) Still used after R2, with effect. Entry 1672 (l.2986-3002) re-ran every repro once on its own build (26 programs, 9 written fresh) and measured PB1317, which the report had only from code reading. The public skills have no registrar role, so 'not yet as a role' holds only for the public skills. State the current rule as R2, not as 'rebuild and re-probe everything'.

theme: Checkpointing, restarts, session and quota limits
title: Session and spend limits kill fleets mid-run

validator.title: Session and spend limits kill fleets mid-run
validator.root_cause: Confirmed by inspection and measurement. The fleet held its decisions only in running agents: DEVLOG 1028 (2026-07-26) records that an absent output file is indistinguishable from work that never ran, and adds per-agent JSON persistence plus a merge that is safe mid-run and marks unverified findings as not actionable. The per-agent form was not yet enough: on 2026-09-02, fifteen refuters that wrote nothing until they finished lost every decision (DEVLOG 1430). That incident produced the per-item JSONL checkpoint this candidate states as the fix.
validator.evidence: The figures match. DEVLOG 906 (2026-07-19): 184 agents, 85 completed, a session-limit outage killed 99. docs/rearchitecture/PHASE-13-plan-vs-spec-review.md line 19: 37 findings UNVERIFIED. DEVLOG 910 (2026-07-19): the resume of wf_099b899f-7eb was killed by the MONTHLY spend limit, 107/119 agent calls failed. Date correction: the events fall on 2026-07-19 (the kills) and 2026-07-26 (the persistence fix). No primary source for a 2026-07-05 start was found.
validator.battle_tested: Yes. Per-item JSONL checkpoints with read-and-skip have been the standing workflow-stage protocol since 2026-09-02 (workstream SKILL.md section 1; agent-fleet SKILL section 4), with no reversal. Measured saves: at the 2026-09-04 fourth pause, batch-3 part B had nine of eleven subjects adjudicated, and the fresh run replayed its .jsonl checkpoints, re-adjudicating only the two whose out- files were missing (DEVLOG 1455/1456). DEVLOG 1449 records a refute fleet stopped on its checkpoints. The 2026-09-23/24 adjudication fleets resumed their STOP-ed refutes from disk (campaign-state memory).
validator.correction: Dates are 2026-07-19 to 2026-07-26. The root cause is sharper than 'no per-agent persistence': a per-agent file written at return (the 07-26 fix) still lost everything on 2026-09-02. The unit of persistence must be the decided item.

refuter.title: Session and spend limits kill fleets mid-run
refuter.reason: The two numbers check out: DEVLOG 906 records 184 agents with 85 completed and 99 killed, the review ledger (line 19) lists 37 findings UNVERIFIED, and DEVLOG 910 records the resume of wf_099b899f-7eb killed by the MONTHLY spend limit with 107 of 119 calls failed. The stated root cause is contradicted by the primary source. It says the fan-out had 'no per-agent persistence'. But ledger section 5 says in so many words 'the journal preserves all completed results', and 910 shows the resume replaying the completed work and running only the missing finders. Nothing already decided was lost. What died was work still in flight. The verify agents ran one finding and one lens each (ledger sections 9 to 24: batches of 5 items in 10 agents), so a per-item or per-agent checkpoint would have saved nothing. The 910 kill came from a monthly billing ceiling, which no checkpoint scheme addresses. The review was actually finished the same day by re-running verification in batches of 10 (ledger sections 9 to 24, 'VERIFICATION COMPLETE'). The per-item JSONL fix answers a different incident: fifteen refuters on 2026-09-02 that wrote nothing to disk (DEVLOG 1430), which is the next candidate's evidence. The per-agent JSON of DEVLOG 1028 was added a week later, in a different fleet (spec reconciliation), as a precaution the owner asked for, not in response to a measured loss. The validator could only vet this by swapping in 1430 as the root cause. The '2026-07-05' start date has no source. Problem, root cause and fix do not form one established chain.

title: The limit kills every live agent at once, landers included

validator.title: The limit kills every live agent at once, landers included
validator.root_cause: Confirmed by observation, repeated. Every cutoff killed all live agents simultaneously, landers included (2026-09-01, 2026-09-02, 2026-09-04 ~17:00, 2026-09-05 14:15, 2026-09-06 ~06:35). The reset hour was read off each 429 and varied: 12:20am and 4:10pm PT (DEVLOG 1430), 2:50pm (09-05) and 8:00am (09-06), per memory feedback_session_usage_winddown.
validator.evidence: Matches memory reference_session_limit_and_resume.md: on 2026-09-01 about 23:xx PT, about 14 concurrent implementer and lander agents plus a 39-agent workflow hit the 429 after roughly 2.5 h, and a main-tree lander died after applying its patch and before its commit. Second cutoff on 2026-09-02 (reset 4:10pm), with finished landings waiting behind one serialized lander. DEVLOG 1430 confirms both cutoffs and the two reset times.
validator.battle_tested: Yes. The restart procedure (read the reset time, check main's state, then fresh agents in landing order) was used on 2026-09-04 (DEVLOG 1456), 2026-09-05 (DEVLOG 1542: the restart found all six train-13 cluster commits already in the dead lander's worktree), 2026-09-06 twice (trains 17 and 18, DEVLOG 1556/1559) and 2026-09-21 (wave 42). 'Land finished work first' is standing practice (MANDATORY-PRACTICES L-rules; the rolling wave starts trains as branches finish), with no reversal.
validator.correction: The 'git status on main' step mattered only while landers applied patches in the main checkout. Since 2026-09-02, landers work in worktrees and land through push-main.sh, so the check now reads the dead lander's worktree and STATUS.md. The memory file's description still says 'resets 12:20am'; its body corrects this.

refuter.reason: The observation itself is confirmed. So that step was exercised once, at most, for its stated purpose, and the validator's own correction concedes the check now reads the worktree. theme: Checkpointing, restarts, session and quota limits
title: Resuming a long transcript costs more than a fresh agent reading a checkpoint

validator.title: Resuming a long transcript costs more than a fresh agent reading a checkpoint
validator.root_cause: Established by measurement and inspection. The cost law tokens = 0.115*T + 0.00031*T^2 was fitted over n = 239 agents and refitted independently (PROCESS-REVIEW-2026-09-04.md; workstream SKILL.md section 2). Under it, a turn at T = 300 costs about 2.6 times a turn at T = 0, because the whole context is re-read on every turn. The loss half was measured directly: on 2026-09-02, fifteen refuters that wrote nothing until they finished lost every decided rule when the window closed (DEVLOG 1430).
validator.evidence: Matches DEVLOG 1430 (2026-09-02 17:08) and memory reference_session_limit_and_resume.md (owner correction 2026-09-02 16:25): 28 concurrent agents burned about 20 % of a session window in 11 minutes; about 50 had exhausted the previous window in about 2.5 h; resuming eight 300-turn implementers at once was the costliest action of the day. Caveat: the 20 %-in-11-minutes burn came from resuming the eight implementers and the fifteen refuters together, so it is not an isolated measurement of transcript resume. The candidate is right that the public-skill eval for 'fresh vs resume' was dropped: evals/README.md, W/OUT 1.00, the baseline already chose correctly.
validator.battle_tested: Yes. 'Fresh agent from the checkpoint' has been the restart rule for every cutoff since: 2026-09-04 (DEVLOG 1456), 2026-09-05 (DEVLOG 1542), 2026-09-06 trains 17 and 18 (DEVLOG 1556/1559), 2026-09-21 wave 42, and the wave-43 outage. Measured effects: wave 42, re-dispatched from WIP checkpoints, cost 3.30 M against wave 41's 3.70 M for the same shape (DEVLOG 1628; campaign-state memory). After the wave-43 outage the checkpoint-resumed implementers finished in about 45 and about 95 turns, against about 150 fresh. No reversal was found.
sources: E:/COBOL/docs/rearchitecture/evidence/PROCESS-REVIEW-2026-09-04.md (cost law, 44.6 M vs 40.3 M, lander 295.9 M vs 140 M)
validator.correction: The resume-versus-fresh comparison is modelled from the fitted cost law. It was never measured head to head. Of the checkpoint parts, the WIP commit is the reliable one: 3 of 14 finished real branches (21 %) ended with a STATUS.md that did not describe their own last commit, with no crash involved (2026-09-28 stamped-handoff scale test, kb/Work/PB1701). The STATUS-AT stamp that detects this dates from 2026-09-28 and is not yet vetted. Its enforcing hook was withdrawn from the public skill the same day.

refuter.title: Resuming a long transcript costs more than a fresh agent reading a checkpoint
refuter.reason: The comparison in the title was never measured, and the validator concedes it is 'modelled from the fitted cost law ... never measured head to head'. The only measurement cited, 20% of a window in 11 minutes (DEVLOG 1430 and the owner correction in the memory file), came from eight resumed implementers and fifteen refuters that had written nothing to disk, all resumed together. It does not isolate the cost of resuming a transcript. The 'battle-tested' figures compare the wrong things. Wave 42's 3.30 M against wave 41's 3.70 M, and the wave-43 implementers resumed from checkpoints finishing in about 45 and about 95 turns against about 150, both measure a fresh agent from a checkpoint against a fresh agent from scratch. Neither measures it against resuming the transcript. The same memory block records that wave 43's checkpoint resume cost 1.75 M on top of the 1.73 M the killed attempt had already spent: 'the outage roughly doubled the price'. The project's own numbers also make the claim conditional. PROCESS-REVIEW line 238 puts an implementer's fixed cost at about 70 turns, and the cost law is 0.1154T + 0.000309T². Under those, resuming a 300-turn transcript is cheaper than a fresh agent that re-pays about 70 turns of orientation whenever fewer than about 68 turns remain. That is why the doctrine itself says to resume via SendMessage when the agent is 'within a step of finishing' (workstream SKILL section 1; agent-fleet section 12 step 4). The public skill only says 'often'. The unqualified title overstates this. The checkpoint half of the fix has also failed in practice. PB201's STATUS.md was stale by three checkpoints (DEVLOG 1456). Wave 43 group D's STATUS.md said 'finished' on an ungated branch (campaign-state memory). In the 2026-09-28 scale test, 3 of 14 branches (21%) ended with a stale STATUS.md with no crash involved. The remedy, the STATUS-AT stamp enforced by status_guard, is explicitly unvetted: it was withdrawn from the public skill on 2026-09-28 (MANDATORY-PRACTICES P4; claude-skills commit 4423ad0). Missing: a head-to-head measurement of resume against fresh-from-checkpoint, and a vetted, reliable checkpoint.

title: A workflow run resumes only in the process that ran it

validator.title: A workflow run resumes only in the process that ran it
validator.root_cause: Observed once and never reproduced. On 2026-09-20 a reboot killed the process that owned run wf_c18987cb-f4c, and the run could not be resumed with resumeFromRunId. That is the only primary record (campaign-state memory, 09-20 15:30 and 09-21 11:07 blocks; DEVLOG 1628: 'a suspended run cannot be resumed across processes'). No error text was recorded and no controlled retry was made. 'Bound to the process' is an inference from one failure. The '(and session)' half has no source I could find.
validator.evidence: Partly confirmed. '6 worktrees preserved, 0 implementers redone' matches memory: six predecessor worktrees wf_c18987cb-f4c-1..6 were verified present, clean and carrying WIP checkpoints and STATUS.md, and 'no implementer had completed, so nothing is re-done twice'. The 2026-09-04 claim ('earlier, a run could not be resumed from another session') is not supported. DEVLOG 1456 shows the 09-04 streams re-dispatched fresh by choice, and the memory planned a resumeFromRunId for wf_c48098e4-51b, with no failure recorded. Counter-observation: the same memory records that a workflow survived a /clear, which is the same process.
validator.battle_tested: The workaround is battle-tested. A new run that reads stage inputs from disk and merges the predecessor branches through RESUME lines was used on 2026-09-04 (DEVLOG 1456), on 2026-09-21 for wave 42 (3.30 M, zero errors, DEVLOG 1628) and after the wave-43 outage. The limitation itself is not: one observation.
sources: E:/claude-skills/skills/agent-fleet/SKILL.md section 12 step 4 (still says a workflow resumes from its run id, with no caveat)
validator.correction: State it as an observation: after the owning process died (a reboot), resumeFromRunId did not work, so design every stage to rebuild from disk and re-dispatch as a new run. Drop the 2026-09-04 and 'another session' claims.
validator.missing: A reproduction of the run-id resume failure: same session after a process restart, and a different live session, with the error text recorded. A source for the 2026-09-04 cross-session failure.

theme: Checkpointing, restarts, session and quota limits
title: A continuation after a kill confirms, it never re-applies

validator.title: A continuation after a kill confirms, it never re-applies
validator.root_cause: The kills are confirmed: session limits killed three train landers mid-landing, train 13 (2026-09-05 14:15) and trains 17 and 18 (2026-09-06). But the lesson drawn from them is contradicted by two of the three trains the candidate cites as evidence.
validator.evidence: Only train 13 matches the candidate. DEVLOG 1542 and the train-13 paragraph (line ~9807) record that the continuation lander confirmed every verdict batch by dry run: seven dry runs, rows changed 0, GAP 2820 -> 2820, and build_inventory.py left traceability-inventory.json byte-identical. Train 17 (DEVLOG 1556): the first lander died part-way through row 3. The continuation 'reset to row 2's boundary and redid row 3 cleanly', so it re-did the partial step. Train 18 (DEVLOG 1559): the continuation 'discarded the killed lander's half-applied traceability-inventory hunk, and re-applied all four verdict batches with record_verdicts.py on the merged tree'.
validator.battle_tested: The accurate form, 'finish from the last COMPLETE checkpointed step, discard and redo a partial step', was exercised three times and worked each time (one step lost, nothing repeated, as DEVLOG 1556 puts it). The candidate's 'never re-applies' form was not what happened in two of three cases.
validator.contradiction: DEVLOG 1556 (train 17 continuation reset to row 2's boundary and redid row 3) and DEVLOG 1559 (train 18 continuation discarded the half-applied inventory hunk and re-applied all four verdict batches).
validator.correction: A continuation resumes from the last complete checkpoint. It confirms steps that finished; record_verdicts is idempotent, so a finished batch's dry run shows 0 rows changed. It discards and redoes a step the kill left half-done, and it never promotes a WIP commit to main.

theme: Checkpointing, restarts, session and quota limits
title: Wind down before the limit instead of riding into it

validator.title: Wind down before the limit instead of riding into it
validator.root_cause: The failure is confirmed: three fleet-killing 429s in about two days (2026-09-04 ~17:00, 2026-09-05 14:15, 2026-09-06 ~06:35), each killing every live agent. The stated root cause and fix, a hand-kept running tally against a fixed per-window token budget, did not survive as the mechanism. The tally's calibration moved: the 2026-09-06 budget of ~8 M per window became ~10.6 M per window on 2026-09-13. A tally-based estimate then read 57 % weekly when the meter read 90 % (2026-09-19). MANDATORY-PRACTICES now makes the claude.ai meter the pacing authority (O3: read the meter before every dispatch; O5: the hand-kept tally could not attribute cost, and the meter stays the pacing authority).
validator.evidence: Matches memory feedback_session_usage_winddown.md: owner 2026-09-06 08:50 PDT, after the third fleet-killing 429 in two days; 7-9 agents died each time; landers were killed mid-landing; each restart cost about an hour of assessment; about 8-9 M subagent tokens over about 3.5 h (03:07-06:35) exhausted one window; 9 agents x ~300 k = 2.7 M per batch. The STOP file dates from 2026-09-22 (DEVLOG 1637). The ~75 % finishers-only and ~85-90 % stop thresholds became the owner's session soft/hard lines (70/90, 2026-09-12) and the ~85 % session STOP.
validator.battle_tested: The wind-down half is battle-tested. No fleet-killing 429 appears in the DEVLOG or the campaign-state memory after 2026-09-06, while the fleet ran near its limits for three weeks. Graceful stops recur: 2026-09-12 'stopped for the week on quota, losing nothing', 2026-09-22 train-50 lander (DEVLOG 1650), 2026-09-23 and 2026-09-24 STOP-file stops, and a pace cron that creates STOP through 2026-09-28. The tally half is not: it was replaced by meter reading after its estimates failed.
validator.correction: Keep 'wind down before the limit': at a soft line dispatch only finishers, and at a hard line create the STOP file. But drive it from the real meter, not a hand-kept tally against a fixed token budget, whose calibration drifted and misled.
validator.missing: Evidence that the tally itself, rather than meter reading plus the STOP file, prevented a kill. As written, the root cause ('no running usage tally') and its fix are superseded by O3/O5.
validator.contradiction: MANDATORY-PRACTICES O3/O5 (meter is the pacing authority; the tally could not attribute cost) and reference_quota_meter_artifact.md 2026-09-19 (a tally-derived estimate of 57 % against a true 90 %).

theme: Checkpointing, restarts, session and quota limits
title: A quota estimate from a stale calibration is worse than none

validator.title: A quota estimate from a stale calibration is worse than none
validator.root_cause: The incident is confirmed by the owner's meter reading. On 2026-09-19 the orchestrator's estimate said 57 % weekly when the meter read 90 %, because it used the 0.66 M-per-weekly-point rate calibrated under the September-13 boost. Memory feedback_landings_only records that the boost ended on 2026-09-13. The broader claim, that the rate 'drifts from week to week' and so explains the calibration spread, is not established. Two same-day stretches on 2026-09-19 gave ~0.11 and ~0.25 M per point, so part of the spread is short-stretch measurement on a meter that reads in whole percents. The memory itself warns that a single early reading over-states the rate.
validator.evidence: The listed calibrations exist. 0.66 M per point (09-13, boosted); ~0.11 M and ~0.25 M (09-19, reference_quota_meter_artifact.md); ~0.35 M and ~0.4 M (09-20); ~0.55 M (DEVLOG 1635, 2026-09-22, 'fitted on Opus 5'). The 57 % vs 90 % figure is exact.
validator.battle_tested: Reading the real meter (via Claude in Chrome since 2026-09-23; O3) has been used before dispatches through 2026-09-28, for example DEVLOG 2026-09-28 'Weekly meter at dispatch: 23 %', with pace crons that read the meter and create STOP. That is about five days of use and no measured effect. The stated rule, 'never plan on an extrapolated rate', is not the practice: pacing still projects each dispatch's cost from a per-wave rate. Examples: 'a full wave ~9 pts (~3.7 M at ~0.4 M/pt) projects to ~22 %' on 2026-09-21, and 'projected weekly % after it' in the 2026-09-23/25 pacing rule.
validator.correction: Read the meter before every dispatch, and treat a projected cost as a projection re-checked against the next reading, never as the state. Recalibrate after any boost or model change. Do not attribute the calibration spread to weekly drift alone.
validator.missing: Evidence that meter-first pacing prevented an overrun or under-spend that estimates would have caused, beyond the single 2026-09-19 incident. An explanation of the calibration spread that separates rate drift from whole-percent measurement noise.

validator.title: Pace to the weekly budget, not only the session window
validator.root_cause: Both incidents are confirmed. 2026-09-13: six implementers per five-hour window cost ~16 % of the weekly limit, which would have exhausted the week six days before the 09-20 reset; the weekly meter read 48 % after one day (memory feedback_landings_only_2026-09-13.md). 2026-09-25: the day schedule derived from the one-time free reset (Thu 49 %, Fri 74 %, Sat 98 %) was wrong; the owner corrected it, and the orchestrator had stopped Friday at 74 % with ~12 points unspent (project_owner_decision_weekly_pacing_2026-09-23.md).

'~16 % per window' (09-13); 'a full wave ~9 pts ~65 % of one day's 14.3 % allowance' (reference_quota_meter_artifact.md, measured 2026-09-20); '~12 points' (weekly-pacing memory, 2026-09-25 correction). sources: E:/COBOL/DEVLOG.md (2026-09-26/27 trains below the band before the weekly reset)
validator.correction: The allowance is cumulative from the Sunday 03:00 reset (end of day N = N/7), and unused allowance rolls forward. It is not a fixed per-day slice, and not a schedule re-derived from a mid-week reset.

title: A graceful STOP file works where messaging cannot

validator.title: A graceful STOP file works where messaging cannot
validator.root_cause: Confirmed by inspection and by the failures it replaced. Workflow agents cannot be messaged (workstream SKILL.md section 1). Before the STOP file, the limit killed agents mid-step: trains 13, 17 and 18 had landers killed mid-landing (DEVLOG 1542/1556/1559), and on 2026-09-06 the orchestrator had to hand-commit every dead worktree's dirt as a WIP checkpoint (campaign-state memory). The rule was adopted 2026-09-22 on the owner's instruction 'attempt to not lose work due to a quota kill' (DEVLOG 1637).
validator.evidence: Matches the primary sources. DEVLOG 1650 (2026-09-22): train 50's lander 'had stopped gracefully before push-main for the 19:40 session reset', and its report said NOT LANDED. DEVLOG 1672 (2026-09-24): Registrar 14f stopped on the STOP file with its work in a WIP commit, and a finisher completed it. DEVLOG 1669: Registrar 14c stopped the same way, and a finisher merged its checkpoint branch and re-recorded the batch.
validator.battle_tested: Yes, repeatedly since 2026-09-22. Wave 47 was the first dispatch with the STOP line. Session stops using STOP followed on 2026-09-22 19:01, 2026-09-23 11:17 and 2026-09-24 05:04, with the stopped refutes and registrars resumed from disk that day. The lane-3 templates honor args.stopFile (DEVLOG 1664). A pace cron creates STOP at the weekly or session line through 2026-09-28. It is in force as MANDATORY-PRACTICES P3 and is checked by check_practices.py. No quota kill of a working agent is recorded after its adoption, and it was never reversed. (The 2026-09-28 wave-70 stop was for hung model calls, not quota.)

refuter.title: A graceful STOP file works where messaging cannot
refuter.reason: All four criteria are independently confirmed. (1) Root cause, confirmed by inspection and by the failure it replaced. DEVLOG 1637 (2026-09-22) records that workflow agents cannot be messaged and gives the owner's words 'attempt to not lose work due to a quota kill'. Before the STOP file, the only lever was a hard TaskStop or the limit itself, and landers were killed mid-step (DEVLOG 1542, 1556, 1559). (2) Evidence re-checked. DEVLOG 1650: train 50's lander 'had stopped gracefully before push-main for the 19:40 session reset', and its report says NOT LANDED. The memory log shows STOP created at 19:01 and the lander stopped at 19:38 with all seven clusters gated GREEN. DEVLOG 1669: the registrar was 'stopped by the STOP file', and a finisher merged its checkpoint branch. DEVLOG 1672: Registrar 14f 'stopped on the STOP file ... with its work in a WIP commit'. (3) Not reversed. The rule is P3 in MANDATORY-PRACTICES. It is enforced by check_practices.py, which checks the STOP line in the lander, implementer, lane-3 and rolling-wave templates. wf_rolling_wave.js carries it, and the public agent-fleet section 5 and brief-template.md 'Stop rules' carry it too. The known caveats refine it without contradicting it: a STOPPED result must not be replayed through resumeFromRunId, and CONFORMS rows from STOPPED refuters must not be recorded (campaign-state memory, day-2 stop block). (4) Battle-tested. Graceful stops were used on 2026-09-22 19:01, 2026-09-23 11:17 and 2026-09-24 05:04, and again through the pace crons to 2026-09-28. Each time the stopped work was finished from disk by finishers. No session-limit kill of a working agent appears in the DEVLOG after Entry 1637 (grep of every later entry). The 2026-09-28 wave-70 stop was for hung model calls, not quota.

validator.root_cause: The problems were measured. 2026-09-02: 28 concurrent Opus agents burned ~20% of a session window in 11 min, and three finished clusters sat unlanded behind one lander (Entry 1430, line ~13570). 2026-09-05: the 3-slot lane ran at full utilization while the lander idled about half the time; twelve consecutive file-I/O clusters forced a six-conflict mid-flight merge of ~70 turns (Entry 1523; PB327 ran 217 turns). title: Never merge structured data textually

validator.title: Never merge structured data textually
validator.root_cause: Confirmed by inspection, three times. Train 33 (Entry 1604, 2026-09-13): a both-sides merge of tests/version-matrix/cobol-words.json produced one object with duplicate keys; json.load accepted it and silently dropped BOOLEAN, caught when gen-cobol-words printed total=123 where 124 was due. Train 40 (Entry 1618, 2026-09-19): a textual both-sides merge of 85/manifest.json produced two 'enabled' keys; json.load keeps the last, so 96 goldens would have vanished with validators green. Train 50 (Entry 1651, 2026-09-22): a union resolution left pb854_eop_perform_when three times, and CI's shard guard saw 8073 of 8074 discovered because --list-tests counts duplicates and execution does not.
validator.evidence: Counts match: 96; 123 vs 124; 8,073 vs 8,074. Correction: the 123/124 case is itself the duplicate-key mechanism, not a separate 'dropped one element'.
validator.battle_tested: Sustained use, with no reversal and no recurrence found after the 2026-09-22 loader fix. Set-merge with element-count checks recurs in later trains (lines ~6476, ~5973, ~4563, ~3945, ~3574, ~1557, ~881, and train 70b line ~78). Generated files are regenerated rather than merged (DIAGNOSTICS.md and the construct .g.cs files come back byte-identical, e.g. Entry 1592, train 28, line ~7887, and trains 48 and 57). Verdict batches are re-applied with record_verdicts.py on every train (L6). ConformanceCorpus.Load throws on duplicates, and its failure branch was proven with a planted pb249 duplicate.

refuter.title: Never merge structured data textually
refuter.reason: The incidents and the mechanism are confirmed. The absolute prescription is not the practice that was sustained and battle-tested. Confirmed: in Entry 1604 (train 33), a both-sides merge of cobol-words.json produced duplicate keys and silently dropped BOOLEAN, caught when gen-cobol-words printed total=123 where 124 was due. The candidate's 'dropped one element' is accurate, and the validator's 'correction' is not needed. In Entry 1618 (train 40), two 'enabled' keys in 85/manifest.json would have lost 96 goldens. In Entry 1651 (train 50), a union resolution left pb854_eop_perform_when three times, and CI saw 8073 of 8074. Against 'never', the project's own later landings merged structured data textually and made it safe by verifying: - Entry 1625 (train 43, 2026-09-21): eighteen conflicts were 'resolved as keep-both and then VERIFIED'. The brief's lesson is quoted there as 'a JSON list conflict taken on both sides is silently lossy', and 'the textual merge of traceability-inventory.json had preserved every cluster's rows exactly'. - Entry 1651 (train 50): 'The inventory merged textually', checked per row. - Entry 1650 (train 51), Entry 1666 (train 59), Entry 1742 (train 66) and Entry 1758 (train 70b): manifests were resolved as 'both sides taken' or 'unioned as whole elements', with count and uniqueness checks. The fix the candidate names, set-merge by script (train 40), lapsed within three days: train 50's union triplicated an entry, and only CI caught it. The protections that actually held are: regenerating generated files; L6 (verdict batches re-applied, never merged as JSON hunks); element-count and uniqueness verification of every merged list; and ConformanceCorpus.Load throwing on duplicates. That guard was fired once by a planted duplicate and has not fired on a real merge since. A vettable restatement: 'a textual merge of structured data can silently drop or duplicate elements. Never trust one: regenerate generated files, re-apply recorded batches rather than merging them, verify every merged list's count and uniqueness, and make loaders reject duplicates.' Missing for the candidate as written: evidence that avoiding textual merges, rather than verifying them, is what the project sustained and what helped.

title: Agent cost is quadratic in turns, so cap every transcript and split instead of extending

validator.title: Agent cost is quadratic in turns, so cap every transcript and split instead of extending
validator.root_cause: Measured twice on 2026-09-04: fitted and independently refitted as 0.1154*T + 0.000309*T^2 over n = 239 (PROCESS-REVIEW-2026-09-04 line 209; cache-read = 97.6 % of all tokens). I re-checked it on today's Opus 5.5 transcripts with scripts/telemetry/workflow_metrics.py, n = 175 agents of 5-220 turns: tokens(M) = 0.078*T + 0.00096*T^2. The quadratic model has SSE 1,385 against 3,779 for the best linear-only fit. So superlinear cost in turns reproduces on independent data.
validator.evidence: Matches the source: n = 239, 5.62 B tokens, 18 agents at >= 250 turns burned 39 %, and a 150-turn cap models 2.19 B -> 1.21 B (45 % less). Three weekly-limit pauses in six days: PROCESS-REVIEW line 120ff and section 2.0.
validator.battle_tested: Yes. The owner adopted the caps on 2026-09-04 (decision 2). They are in force as MANDATORY-PRACTICES P5 (160 read-only, 220 implementer, split at the cap) and in the role maxTurns, and have been used in every wave through wave 70 with SPLIT and finisher agents. There is no reversal. Measured compliance: 0 of 175 recent agents exceeded 220 turns (maximum 220), against 18 of 239 at >= 250 turns before the caps. fix_clusters.py's cap of 5 notes also derives from the law (DEVLOG line ~713).
validator.contradiction: DEVLOG Entry 1635 (2026-09-22) demoted the coefficients and the 160/220 caps to 'hypotheses to re-measure against the meter on the first 5.5 wave, not constants'. That caveat concerns the coefficients only. The quadratic shape survives the refit above.
validator.correction: The coefficients are specific to the model and harness. On Opus 5.5 with the 1-hour cache, the refit is ~0.078*T + 0.00096*T^2 (n = 175, 2026-09-28): the quadratic term is ~3x steeper, and a 220-turn agent costs ~60 M rather than 40 M. The '45 % less' figure is a model of the same turns re-split. It does not include the orientation cost of each successor, so it is an upper bound.

refuter.title: Agent cost is quadratic in turns, so cap every transcript and split instead of extending
refuter.reason:
(1) The mechanism is confirmed only for ALL-tokens. I inspected six current transcripts of 206-220 turns: per-turn cache_read grows roughly linearly (e.g. 64K at turn 10 to 397K at turn 220), so cumulative cache reads are quadratic.

(2)+(3) FAIL. DEVLOG Entry 1635 (2026-09-22) demotes 'the quadratic turn-cost law and the 160/220 turn caps' to 'hypotheses to re-measure against the meter on the first 5.5 wave, not constants'. That covers the law and the caps. The validator's reading, that it concerns the coefficients only, contradicts the text. No later entry records that re-measurement, and PB1700 (the backfill of the cost-law record) is still status: open. My refit on current transcripts (n=176, 5-220 turns) gives 0.0826*T + 0.00093*T^2. So the learning's stated law does not hold for the model in use, yet SKILL.md section 2 and P5 still carry 0.115/0.00031. The quadratic comes entirely from cache reads. Fresh (non-cached) tokens fit linearly (b = -0.00001). At API cache-read weight (0.1x), the quadratic share at 220 turns falls from 71% to 51%. The premise 'use all-tokens, that is what the weekly limit consumes' (PROCESS-REVIEW line 208) is asserted and was never measured. The project's own meter calibrations (0.1-0.66 M per weekly point) are in harness agent tokens, about 1% of all-tokens. The 'independent refit' re-fit the same shared usage.json (line 163), not independent data. The raw data and probe scripts were not kept (PB1700 says so; they are not in git), so the 39% and 2.19->1.21 B figures cannot be re-derived. On the surviving 2026-09-01..04 transcripts (n=294), agents at 250+ turns hold 19.7% of all-tokens against 21.3% of fresh tokens, so the quadratic does not explain their outsized share.

title: Command chaining: a targeted rule, not a blanket ban

validator.title: Command chaining: a targeted rule, not a blanket ban
validator.root_cause: Mis-stated. With `dotnet test ... && git commit`, the commit runs only when the test exits 0, so '&&' alone cannot commit on a failing run. The documented false green (DEVLOG Entry 1140, 2026-08-02) was `dotnet test ... | tail -2 && git commit`: the PIPELINE's status is tail's, so '&&' tested tail. The general mechanism is exit status masked by a pipe or by ';', or a test run that exits 0 with nothing run (the vstest empty-filter trap). It is not '&&' itself.
validator.evidence: DEVLOG Entry 1739 (2026-09-27 12:48) records P14, hook rule 5 in forbidden_commands.py and 'Self-test: 35/35', and the rejection of the blanket ban on the ground that it adds turns. The claimed saving from not banning chains was never measured, as the candidate says. Memory feedback_gate_on_the_verdict_line says the chained commit recurred and 'red runs were pushed anyway, twice'.
validator.battle_tested: No. The rule was adopted 2026-09-27, about one day before this validation. Only the hook's self-test (35/35) exists. There is no production record of blocks, false positives, or turns added or saved.
validator.correction: The false green came from `dotnet test ... | tail -2 && git commit` (DEVLOG 1140): a pipe masked the verdict. The chain's operator did not.
validator.missing: Production evidence across later waves: how many times the hook blocked a real chain after a verdict, the false-positive rate, and a measurement that the targeted form costs fewer turns than a blanket ban.

title: Wall-clock assertions measure the host, and so does a same-run timing ratio

validator.title: Wall-clock assertions measure the host, and so does a same-run timing ratio
validator.root_cause: Confirmed by measurement in both steps. PB1590 (Entry 1708, 2026-09-25): DeepNestingTests held a whole compile, Roslyn included, to 20 s. It went red twice on a loaded hosted Windows runner, at 26.4 s for a 1-second compile, with no compiler change. PB1600 (Entry 1718, 2026-09-26): the replacement, a same-run stopwatch ratio, failed at 36x against a bound of 30 on untouched code, because 'the small reading (milliseconds) was dominated by one preemption'.
validator.evidence: Matches: the 20 s ceiling, 26.4 s, the owner's quote, the first red that was re-run instead of fixed, and 36x against 30. One claim is wrong: 'Six tests were reshaped to count work'. Entry 1708 removed or reshaped six ceilings, but only DeepNestingTests counted work. CobolTimingTests now observes the effect, PictureCompositionTests became a ratio (it counted work only after PB1600), and the CldrLocaleLoader ceiling and the two FixedForm ceilings were simply removed.
validator.battle_tested: Yes. NoWallClockAssertionDriftTests runs in every Unit gate, and it found the PictureComposition ceiling that the first grep missed. The planted regression turned DeepNestingTests red in 1 s (749 lists against 9). PB1600 removed the ratio and tightened the drift test. Every train review since has checked changed tests for time limits (Entry 1718; DEVLOG ~890), and the DEVLOG records no timing red after Entry 1718.
validator.contradiction: None against the candidate. One secondary source is stale: memory feedback_no_wall_clock_tests.md still lists 'a same-run growth ratio' as acceptable. PB1600 reversed that, and the candidate follows the later source.
validator.correction: Six wall-clock ceilings were removed or reshaped (counting work, observing the effect, or dropping the ceiling), not six tests reshaped to count work.

refuter.title: Wall-clock assertions measure the host, and so does a same-run timing ratio
refuter.reason: The facts check out, but the ratio half of the lesson is not battle-tested, and the fix the candidate says is 'in the skills' still teaches the refuted premise. EVIDENCE: Entry 1708 has the 20 s ceiling, 26.4 s for a 1-second compile, red twice, the first red re-run instead of fixed, and the owner quote. Entry 1718 and kb/Work/PB1600.md have 36x against a bound of 30 on untouched code; gates 1, 2 and 4 on the same tree were green. The candidate's 'Six tests were reshaped to count work' is wrong. Of the six, only DeepNestingTests counted work. CobolTimingTests observes the effect, PictureComposition became a ratio, and the Cldr and two FixedForm ceilings were removed. WHY NOT VETTED. (a) The candidate names the fix as '[review] Determinism check and pr-test-analyzer: count the work, not the time'. But E:\claude-skills\agents\pr-test-analyzer.md lines 89-90 still list 'a growth ratio of two readings taken in the same run ... load that slows both readings alike cannot move a ratio' as a deterministic replacement. That is verbatim the premise the candidate calls REVERSED. E:\claude-skills\skills\review\SKILL.md line 89 also still recommends 'a growth ratio of two readings taken in the same run'. The project's own .claude/skills/review/SKILL.md, last edited 2026-09-28 in 6c2487b4f (after PB1600), still says 'or a growth RATIO of two readings in the same run. `NoWallClockAssertionDriftTests` enforces it mechanically'. So does memory feedback_no_wall_clock_tests.md. The eval grader review-wall-clock-ceiling accepts 'growth ratio' as a passing answer. (b) PB1600 states that the drift test CANNOT detect a timestamp ratio: 'the rule against the ratio shape lives in the drift test's summary and docs/DRIFT_RULES.md, not in its pattern'. Even that summary is self-contradictory: it lists 'a growth ratio' as an allowed property and then says a ratio of stopwatch readings is NOT safe. So nothing mechanical enforces the ratio half. The validator's 'PB1600 ... tightened the drift test' overstates what PB1600 did, which was a summary change only. (c) The final form (count the work, no ratio) landed 2026-09-26 and has been exercised exactly once, in PB1600 itself. The ceiling drift test (landed 2026-09-25) caught one missed ceiling when it was introduced. Since then no new timing test has been written that would exercise either rule, so 'no timing red after Entry 1718' over about 3 days is an absence, not a measured effect. MISSING for VETTED: the skills the candidate names must stop recommending a same-run ratio, and the no-ratio practice must be exercised across later waves (a ratio caught in review, or a drift or semgrep rule that recognises one) with no recurrence.

title: Ask the source's own witness, not your copy of it

validator.title: Ask the source's own witness, not your copy of it
validator.root_cause: Confirmed by inspection in DEVLOG Entry 1026 (2026-07-26 17:12): the rule-catalog extractor, validated only against specs/ISO_COBOL.md (the copy it parsed), had four bugs that each produced a clean run. The spec's own TOC caught 15 unrecognised singular 'Syntax rule' blocks, and rendering PDF page 95 caught a page mis-attribution and a leaked anchor. 'Self-consistency is not validation - a parser checked only against the artifact it parses will confirm its own mistakes.'
validator.evidence: Figures match Entry 1026 exactly: the denominator moved 2,974 -> 3,210 -> 3,949 -> 2,314 -> 3,247; 601 phantom rules in the one runaway §16.2.2.2 block; 896 rules lost to over-termination; plus 592 contaminated rules (18%), which the candidate omits. The 'inflation reads as thoroughness' quote is verbatim. Correction: 3,247 was not final. Entry 1529 (2026-09-05, PB689) found the catalog still short by SIXTY rules across five clauses (WRITE held 16 of 42 general rules) because every completeness critic, the TOC check included, asked only whether a block yielded SOMETHING. The fix was an independent per-clause count critic (audit_catalog_coverage.py, which shares none of the extractor's segmentation logic) plus CatalogCoverageDriftTests, which fired RED before the fix. The catalog grew 4,311 -> 4,371.
validator.battle_tested: Applied repeatedly with measured effect: Entry 1026 (the TOC and the PDF found four bugs), Entry 1032 (the embedded PDF outline settled heading depth for 1,728 entries; 2,039 headings rewritten), and Entry 1529 (an independent count witness recovered 60 rows the earlier critics missed, with a drift test proven red). No later entry reverses it. The later entry sharpens it: a witness has to compare COUNTS at the right granularity, because a presence check passes a block that yields 16 of 42.
validator.correction: Add that a TOC/presence witness is not enough: Entry 1529 found 60 rules still missing after the TOC check, because it asked 'did the block yield something' rather than 'printed count == held count'. The independent witness has to compare counts per clause and share no logic with the extractor. The denominator is now 4,371, not 3,247.

refuter.title: Ask the source's own witness, not your copy of it
refuter.reason: Entry 1026 (2026-07-26 17:12, line 32226) is reproduced accurately: four extractor bugs; the denominator moved 2,974 -> 3,210 -> 3,949 -> 2,314 -> 3,247; 601 phantom rules; 896 lost; 592 contaminated; and 'inflation reads as thoroughness'. What later entries contradict is the lesson drawn from it, applied to the candidate's own subject, the completeness of the rule catalog. (a) The 'source's own witness' that Entry 1026 made fatal is the TOC critic at scripts/spec/extract_rule_catalog.py:727-743. It reads the TRANSCRIPTION's TOC links, matching the regex '(Syntax|General|Argument|Returned value) rules?' against specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines. So it is a witness drawn from the copy, and it is keyed on the same heading-name vocabulary as the extractor. (b) Entry 1160 (2026-08-03, line 25481) says that guard class is structurally blind: 'The denominator has been short twice - 3,790 -> 3,846 ... -> 3,861 ... each time the repair extended a guard keyed on the heading TEXT ... There is no spelling of that guard which finds it.' The hole was 100 clauses and 460 ordinals, and it was found by a CONTENT-keyed scan of the copy. (c) Entry 1529 (2026-09-05, line 9837): 60 rules were still missing because 'none of the catalog's completeness critics could see it: they all ask did this block yield SOMETHING'. The TOC critic is one of those critics. The witness that worked, audit_catalog_coverage.py and CatalogCoverageDriftTests, 're-deriv[es] the printed count from the transcription', which is the copy, with logic that 'shares none of the extractor's segmentation logic'. Net result: after the '3,247 checked against the canonical PDF' figure (in fact a two-page sample, pp. 95 and 688), real undercounts added 581 rules (3,247 + 222 for Annex A.1 in commit 845836f6a + 321 for formats in 7f12ea014 = 3,790, then 3,790 -> 4,371). The fatal TOC witness caught none of them. The two largest (the 100-clause hole and the 60 rows) were caught by scans of the copy that use independent logic. The validator's 'No later entry reverses it' is therefore false, and its correction still keeps the source-versus-copy framing that 1160 and 1529 refute. What survives is 1529's own statement ('a critic that reuses the machinery it audits cannot see that machinery's bug'), together with count-not-presence and content-keyed-not-name-keyed. That is a different lesson, and it would need to be vetted on its own. Consulting the PDF for content-fidelity questions (the 1027-1030 reconciliation, the 1032 outline) remains sound, but that is not this candidate's claim or fix.

validator.title: Measure before scheduling performance work; record the null results
validator.root_cause: Established by measurement. Entry 1151 (2026-08-03 13:25) profiled per-class durations from the TRX. VersionMatrixTests was 2,015 tests running serially for 780.2 s, and NistDifferentialTests, written down beforehand as 'the obvious suspect', was second (349 tests, 317.3 s). Entry 1426 (2026-09-02 16:21) measured the null for the split and explained it: 'sum-of-test-time / wall measures COLLECTION concurrency, not core utilisation'. The 'idle' cores were busy with internally parallel Roslyn Emit and dotnet children. The after-profile reports 10,469 s instead of 1,948 s of test time for the same work.
validator.evidence: Re-checked, with one refinement. The ~10x prediction (783 s -> ~80 s) came from a measurement, not from pure arithmetic: it rested on the wrong metric. Measured: Conformance 721 s -> 600 s (-17%), Unit 171 s -> 138 s (-19%). The guard regrouping measured 564 s before and 598 s after, and was kept for correctness (Entry 1151). The compile fan-out cap to nproc/2 was withdrawn (Entry 1151 near line 26019; memory feedback_maximize_test_concurrency), and the rule became 'reduce the WORK rather than the parallelism'.
validator.battle_tested: Used across waves with no reversal. The profile from 2026-08-03 re-targeted the work away from the assumed suspect. A13 (2026-09-02) was measured before and after, and its note was set to 'half' rather than 'landed' because of the null. Entry 1426 names the pattern ('twice in this register a concurrency change was kept for correctness rather than speed'). The fleet-optimization experiment records continue the practice of recording nulls.
validator.correction: The failed 10x prediction was not 'arithmetic instead of observation'. It was an observation of the wrong quantity (collection concurrency taken for core utilisation). The practice needs a second clause: check that the measured metric is the resource the change acts on.

refuter.title: Measure before scheduling performance work; record the null results
refuter.reason: The figures are accurate. Entry 1151 (2026-08-03, lines 26045-26067): VersionMatrixTests had 2,015 tests running serially for 780.2 s, and NistDifferentialTests, named 'the obvious suspect', was second at 349 tests and 317.3 s; the guard regrouping measured 564 s before and 598 s after and was kept for correctness; the nproc/2 cap was reverted. Entry 1426: Conformance went 721 -> 600 s (-17%) and Unit 171 -> 138 s (-19%). But the stated root cause of the candidate's central failure is contradicted by the primary source. The candidate says the ~10x prediction failed from 'plausible arithmetic, not observation'. Entry 1426 (line 13878) says 'The measurement was right and the prediction was wrong', and the premise failed because 'sum-of-test-time / wall measures COLLECTION concurrency, not core utilisation' (the after-profile shows 10,469 s versus 1,948 s). In other words, the practice the title prescribes, measuring before scheduling, WAS followed: A13(b) was profiled on 2026-08-03 before the split was scheduled. It did not prevent a miss of roughly 10x. The same happened in A14. Entry 1214 (2026-08-07) measured the step first (run 31238417792) and predicted '~30 -> ~10-14 min'. Entry 1216 measured 23.3 and then 21.4 min: 'case count was a bad proxy twice'. So two of the three performance predictions in the record were made AFTER measuring and still failed. The remedy the record actually supports is different: measure the quantity the change acts on (per-shard minutes rather than counts; core utilisation rather than collection concurrency), then measure after and record a null. The validator concedes the root-cause misstatement in its own correction, so the candidate is not final as written. 'Record the null results' on its own is well exercised (1151 'honest negative', 1216, 1426 and A13 set to 'half'). However, the fleet-optimization experiment records the validator cites for continued practice are all dated 2026-09-28 and have no track record yet. The corrected lesson would need to be re-vetted as its own candidate.

validator.title: A 1-hour prompt cache for roles that wait on gates
validator.root_cause: Confirmed by inspecting transcripts. Gate-waiting agents block in the foreground for about 585 s per re-issue (the 'timeout 580' wait from Entry 1637), which is longer than the 5-minute TTL. With cacheTtl: 1h (R49 rec. 3, 2026-09-25), the request after each such wait reads the whole prefix from cache (~180k-440k tokens) and writes only ~0.5k-2k new tokens. With a 5-minute TTL that prefix would have expired and been written again.

Corrected by my own measurement of transcripts: across 208 subagent transcripts since 2026-09-25, 164 waits longer than 5 minutes were each followed by a cache read, 55.0M read-after-wait tokens in all, with 1h writes 25.0M and 5m writes 2.0M. For the 38 largest 2026-09-27 agents: 115 waits of ~585 s, each followed by ~1k written and ~180k-440k read. Estimated at API cache multipliers (5m write 1.25x, 1h write 2x, read 0.1x), that avoids ~63M base-token units of re-writes against an ~19M premium for 1h writes, a net of ~44M. The locator transcript shows ephemeral_5m=0, so the frontmatter setting takes effect.

refuter.title: A 1-hour prompt cache for roles that wait on gates
refuter.reason: I tried to overturn this and could not; all four criteria hold on my own measurement. (1) ROOT CAUSE REPRODUCED with an in-project control, not only inferred. Workflow-dispatched cobol-clerk agents have no cacheTtl frontmatter; their 14 transcripts wrote to the 5-minute cache only (0.62M w5m, 0 w1h). General-purpose agents also wrote 5m only. Every role with cacheTtl: 1h wrote 1h only, so the frontmatter is what causes the difference. General-purpose agent a8b7b69c (the PB1699 self-host work, 5-minute default) blocked on the Entry-1637 `timeout 580` gate wait three times (587-589 s). After each wait it re-wrote its whole context: 340k-347k tokens written, 0 read. That is the candidate's Problem, reproduced exactly. Against it, implementer and lander agents had 153 waits over 5 minutes (147 of them about 9 minutes long). Every one was a cache hit with about 1k written afterwards (implementer 44.2M read after waits, lander 8.2M). (2) EVIDENCE RE-CHECKED: the validator's 55.0M read after waits and ~25M of 1h writes match. Its 2.0M of 5m writes is now 6.7M, because this run's own general-purpose agents are inside the measured window. The ~44M net at API ratios is arithmetically right (55.0x1.15 - 25.0x0.75). (3) NOT CONTRADICTED: no DEVLOG entry after 1711 reverses it. `git log -S cacheTtl` shows only additions (e105e0833, ae67a74ac). No memory feedback note corrects it. refuter.reason: The title and the stated root cause are contradicted by harness transcripts of worktree-isolated agents (meta.json spawnedWithWorktree: true), and by the project's current templates. MEASURED: across waves 65-70, 27 tool calls by isolated agents that named ANOTHER worktree succeeded. (a) impl-Y-PB1427 (own wf_bf025bee-c67-8) ran `cd /e/COBOL/.claude/worktrees/wf_475f7239-eda-2 2>/dev/null && cat STATUS.md` and got wave-67 group N's STATUS. That is a cd INTO another worktree, which the candidate says is refused. (b) impl-V2-PB1272 (own wf_e9a82a33-6b6-8) ran `cat E:/COBOL/.claude/worktrees/wf_e9a82a33-6b6-5/STATUS.md`: ok. (c) impl-Z-PB1084 (own wf_64d3a01e-a3d-2) ran another worktree's cobol.exe: ok. (d) Another isolated implementer ran `ls` on another worktree: ok. wf_rolling_wave.js successorNote (lines 76-79) and dispatch-spec-implementer.md:79 now TELL isolated successors to read the predecessor worktree's STATUS.md and run status_delta.py on that worktree, so the project relies on isolated agents reaching other worktrees. WHAT THE GUARD ACTUALLY REFUSES: its refusal texts in the transcripts are all about GIT. They read 'names git in a form too complex to verify that it stays inside the worktree' (102 occurrences), 'cannot be shown not to run git' (many shapes), and 'changes directory to the shared checkout (/e/COBOL) before running git' (10). pwsh from the Bash tool is refused because 'what it reads ... cannot be shown not to run git': 9 of 9 such calls refused and 0 succeeded, so that part of the candidate is confirmed. CORRECT LESSON: an isolated agent's git, and any shell the harness cannot prove is not git, must provably stay inside its own worktree. That covers git -C on another tree, cd to the shared checkout before git, and opaque pwsh/bash invocations. Reading, listing, cd-and-read and running binaries in another worktree all work. Take branch content from the shared object store (`git diff <base> <branch>`, `git merge <branch>`), as trains have done continuously. That practice is sound; the lesson's framing is not. Other defects: the brief's cd/EnterWorktree refusal (f704e92a5, 2026-09-02) concerns the SHARED CHECKOUT, not other worktrees. The narrow `git -C <another worktree>` refusal rests on one train-1 observation (Entry 1461); it is consistent with the guard but was never re-measured. 'Verify each implementer worktree is clean before dispatch' has no recorded exercise. lander-brief.md:10-12 still instructs `git -C {IMPL_WORKTREE}`.

validator.root_cause: Confirmed by measurement. kb/Work/PB784.md (filed 2026-09-06) 're-measured on the shared directory itself': one parent session's scratchpad holds all siblings' files. implementer-brief.md:18 names no gate filename, so agents choose generic basenames. The PB712 finisher's gate3.txt collision was still on disk, holding a sibling's audit count (3576 vs its own 3572). PB784 also records which brief sites already interpolate an identity and are safe.
validator.evidence: Matches. PB784: '1034 entries, of which eleven are gate output under a generic basename' (gate.txt, gate1.txt, gate2.txt, gate3.txt, ...). Registrars overwriting scripts: Entry 1667 (2026-09-24) says '`rows.py` overwritten mid-run; this registrar's scripts moved to a private `r14a/` subdirectory', and DEVLOG line 3023 says 'registrars 14e and 14f overwriting each other's scripts in one shared' scratchpad. Finishers overwriting reports: DEVLOG line 4775 (train 48) says 'The implementer branches for N and O had been overwritten in `reports/` by the wave-48 finishers'. The date span 2026-09-06 to 2026-09-24 holds.
validator.battle_tested: No. The structural fix is still OPEN: kb/Work/PB784.md frontmatter reads `status: open`, and the candidate says the per-agent-subdirectory remedy is 'proposed but OPEN'. The only mitigations are ad hoc (registrar 14a moving its own scripts into `r14a/`) and partial (report-path allocation, and the patch/jsonl sites that already interpolate an identity). Collisions kept recurring after PB784 was filed (Entry 1667 on 09-24, train 48), which shows the defect is real and the fix not yet in force.
validator.missing: The fix landing (PB784 closed, with a per-agent scratch subdirectory or an identity-interpolated filename in every brief) and later waves running without a scratchpad collision. Until then the lesson is a confirmed problem with an unproven remedy. Batch status: all 10 candidates in items 1-10 are decided; none is left undecided.

title: An agent that ends its turn kills its own background gate

validator.title: An agent that ends its turn kills its own background gate
validator.root_cause: Confirmed by inspection, twice. DEVLOG Entry 1637 (2026-09-22 11:47, DEVLOG.md:5058-5076): wave 45's five implementers and the train-46 lander returned 'gate PENDING'. Every one of their logs stops mid-leg with no verdict line, and t46/gate.log's mtime is the minute the lander returned. The briefs said run_in_background and STOP. A workflow agent that stops ends its turn, and its background process dies with it. Entry 1639 (DEVLOG.md:4987) records the same kill for the first train-46 lander: 'ended its turn while the whole-assembly gate ran in the background. The harness killed the gate with it'.
validator.evidence: The wave-45 facts match (5 implementers + 1 lander). CORRECTION: '~440 of its 560 tool calls on one-word waits' is a DIFFERENT incident with a different anti-pattern. It was train 40's lander POLLING with idle tool calls (lander-train-brief.md step 7, introduced in commit 86e4df38e, 'lander brief carries the ... no-polling lessons'). It is not a consequence of ending the turn. It is the opposite failure, and it predates 2026-09-22.
validator.battle_tested: Yes. The rule is in workstream SKILL.md lines 58-63, lander-train-brief.md step 7 and public agent-fleet SKILL.md section 5, and has not been reversed. It has run in every wave since (46-70). DEVLOG Entry 1752 (2026-09-28) measures agents blocking in the foreground through ~580 s gate waits, so the timeout-580 blocking pattern is in sustained use. No later 'gate PENDING' or killed-at-turn-end incident is recorded. One caveat: Entry 1644 (DEVLOG.md:4779) says wave-47 O's own gate 'never printed a verdict (no verdict line in w47o/gate1.log)' after the rule existed. Its cause is not recorded, so it neither confirms nor refutes the rule.
validator.correction: The 440-of-560 tool-call figure belongs to train 40's lander (idle polling), not to the wave-45 turn-end kill. Cite it as a separate 'never poll with idle tool calls' lesson.

refuter.title: An agent that ends its turn kills its own background gate
refuter.reason: Upheld with two corrections. (1) ROOT CAUSE, by inspection: DEVLOG 1637 (DEVLOG.md:5058-5076). Wave 45's 5 implementers and the train-46 lander returned 'gate PENDING - still running when the result was forced'. Every log stops mid-leg, t46/gate.log's mtime is the minute the lander returned, and the briefs said run_in_background and STOP. Entry 1639 (:4987) describes the SAME lander, so this is ONE incident of six agents, not two confirmations as the validator says. (2) EVIDENCE: '5 implementers + 1 lander' and 2026-09-22 match. CORRECTION: '~440 of its 560 tool calls on one-word waits' is train 40's lander on 2026-09-19 (lander-train-brief.md step 7; commit 86e4df38e). That commit's fix, 'run it with run_in_background and then STOP and wait for the harness's completion notification', is the very instruction wave 45 followed and died on. The polling figure is the UPSTREAM cause of this lesson, not part of its Problem. (3) NOT CONTRADICTED: the rule entered workstream SKILL.md in 42fd72b82 and was never removed. It is MANDATORY-PRACTICES P2 and agent-fleet SKILL.md section 5. No later entry reports a turn-end kill. Entry 1644 (w47o/gate1.log had no verdict line, and wave 47 ran after the rule) records no cause and was one of up to 17 concurrent gates (Entry 1645), so it neither confirms nor refutes. Entry 1712's '&'-backgrounded push that survived was the orchestrating session, not a workflow agent. (4) BATTLE-TESTED, which I measured in the raw transcripts. In waves 66, 67, the 68 relaunch, 69, 70 and 70b, 36 of 38 agents issued real 'timeout 580' blocking Bash calls and got verdict lines back. The 2 exceptions: one was cancelled after 3 tool calls, the other never returned. 0 agents in any retained workflow returned a PENDING gate_verdict. Entry 1752 independently measured 5-7 blocking silences of 582-585 s per agent in train 69. The rule's side costs (PB1702's build guard failing open during the waits; transcript silence misread as death) were fixed by adapting the watchers, not by reversing the rule.

title: Workflow agents act on the session's latest message, so carry the authorization

validator.title: Workflow agents act on the session's latest message, so carry the authorization
validator.root_cause: Established by inspecting the agents' own returns. All nine cobol-implementers returned BLOCKED and quoted the session's latest user message: 'the user asked a LinkedIn question, not for the COBOL fix lane' (DEVLOG Entry 1746). Quoting the owner's direction in every prompt removed the refusals on relaunch, which is a before/after reproduction of the mechanism.
validator.evidence: Matches DEVLOG Entry 1746 (2026-09-28 00:06): in wave 68, nine implementers returned BLOCKED and made no changes. The relaunched wave wf_e9a82a33-6b6 'ran with it and no agent refused; train 68 landed from it'. The phrase 'The fix is provenance, not persuasion' comes from memory feedback_workflow_agents_need_authorization.md. The incident was on 2026-09-27 (wave 68), and the fix was logged 2026-09-28 00:06.
validator.battle_tested: Yes, in sustained use with no reversal. The authorization argument is in wf_rolling_wave.js (lines 30-34) and public rolling-wave.js (lines 29 and 52). It carried the wave-68 relaunch, the wave-69 finishers (Entry 1747, 'the finisher wave the owner authorized at 00:05 PDT') and wave 70 (Entry 1748). No BLOCKED refusals are recorded since, and this validation workflow's own prompt carries it.

refuter.title: Workflow agents act on the session's latest message, so carry the authorization
refuter.reason: Not upheld. Its EVIDENCE line is contradicted by the raw run data, and the fix's effect was never isolated. (a) '9 of 9 refused' is WRONG. The refused run is wf_bf025bee-c67 (launched 2026-09-28T01:29:32Z). Its journal logs 7 BLOCKED (R, T, U, S, W, X, Z) with agentCount 10. The 10 transcripts show V, Y and U2 got the IDENTICAL LinkedIn relay and did NOT refuse: they worked ~31 min (157, 163 and 178 tool calls) until the orchestrator killed the workflow at 02:01Z. It was 7 of 10, and DEVLOG 1746's 'all nine' is itself wrong. (b) The claimed before/after reproduction is CONFOUNDED. 0 of the 12 relaunch transcripts (wf_e9a82a33-6b6, 02:06Z) contain a '[Workflow harness - user request]' block, while all 10 in the refused run do. The relaunch removed the conflicting relay AND added the authorization, so its 0 refusals cannot be credited to the authorization. (c) ROOT CAUSE confirmed, refined: the harness relays the session's latest user message, including one queued mid-turn. 'Re linked in...' was enqueued at 01:28:28Z and absorbed_mid_turn, one minute before launch, and the harness framed it as 'the user request that triggered this workflow run ... this request wins'. Refusal is not deterministic: the 01:18Z run (wf_8b2b0670-764) had no authorization and an unrelated relay (a pasted 'Fable' note), and 0 of 6 refused. (d) NOT BATTLE-TESTED. Of the authorized launches since, the 68 relaunch had no relay; wave 69's relay was the owner's own authorizing message ('now and land the script fix now too...'); 70b's was 'go ahead with train 70b and the U2 finisher'; this validation run's is 'start the validation run'. Only wave 70 (wf_ae05e6d0-c50) met the failure condition: an unrelated relay 'I still haven't see the draft response', 8 of 8 prompts carrying AUTHORIZATION, and 0 BLOCKED. That is ONE exercise, and the criterion says one is not battle-tested. MISSING: repeated exercise under an unrelated relay, or an A/B with the same unrelated relay run with and without authorization. The count should also be corrected to 7 of 10 in DEVLOG 1746 and in memory feedback_workflow_agents_need_authorization.md.

validator.root_cause: Confirmed by reproduction (DEVLOG Entry 1754, PB1703). Group U's agent died on an API error and agent() REJECTED. The rejection escaped the worker with the slot still counted and no wake-up sent, so U2 (after: U) never became eligible. validator.battle_tested: No. The fix landed on 2026-09-28 at ~11:34 and has been exercised only in simulation. NO-RESULT appears in DEVLOG only in Entry 1754 itself. title: One self-contained input file per agent

validator.title: One self-contained input file per agent
validator.root_cause: Observed by reconciliation. DEVLOG Entry 442 (commit de36306d1, 2026-06-07): the 'read element [k] of the config' dispatch 'double-processed 4 clusters and skipped 5 entirely', which was caught 'by reconciling returned canonicals against the cluster map'. Re-running the 5 missing clusters with one input file per agent was 'robust'.
validator.evidence: The figures (4 double-processed, 5 skipped) match DEVLOG.md:49965-49969 exactly. The date is 2026-06-07, so 'June 2026' is correct.
validator.battle_tested: The practice has been used continuously since then with no reversal. The seven reader agents each had their own input file (DEVLOG.md:21429). A fan-out of one agent per function gave each its OWN input file (:28072). scripts/spec/phase_b_batch.py writes one self-contained input file per subject (DEVLOG 1130), and templates/build_lane1_inputs.py writes one file per golden-writer. One later failure refined the rule rather than reversing it: lane 2 (2026-09-25) reused lane 1's bare slugs, and one agent drafted 12 foreign rows from another lane's copy (build_lane1_inputs.py header). So input-file slugs must be unique across lanes. The practice is in agent-fleet SKILL.md section 2 and in memory feedback_agent_dispatch.md.
validator.correction: Add the 2026-09-25 refinement: input-file names (slugs) must be unique across every lane ever run, or an agent may read another lane's copy.

refuter.title: One self-contained input file per agent
refuter.reason: (1) DEVLOG Entry 442 (commit de36306d1, 2026-06-07) records the failure. It was found by checking the returned canonicals against the cluster map: 4 clusters were processed twice and 5 were skipped. The 5 were re-run with one file per agent and succeeded. That agents miscounted the index is the log's own reading of that check, not a reproduction, but the effect itself was measured. (2) The figures (4, 5) and the date (June 2026) match. (3) Nothing reverses it. Entry 1713 (2026-09-25) is a failure of the per-agent-file practice itself: a lane-2 writer read lane 1's committed copy that had the same slug, producing 12 foreign drafts and 0 of its own 13 rows. It was fixed with lane-unique slugs, which refines the practice rather than reversing it. The same entry shows that checking by count (119/120) hid a wholly wrong file, and only a per-slug set comparison exposed it. (4) Used again and again since: seven reader agents each with their own input file (DEVLOG:21429), one agent per function (:28072), page_workunit.py units 'with no shared index to miscount' (:32170), a one-file-per-agent refactor (:38381), phase_b_batch.py (:27268) and build_lane1_inputs.py. Add to the text: slugs must be unique across lanes, and returns are checked by item identity (a set comparison), not by count.

refuter.title: Anything a later session needs must live in the repository
refuter.reason: The principle is sound, and criteria 1, 3 and 4 largely hold. Criterion 2 fails: the candidate's problem and evidence lines misstate the primary sources in three places, and one of them turns the story upside down. (a) 'A decision-complete plan lived in an off-repo temp directory and was lost' is contradicted. On 2026-06-11, Entry 579 folded /e/tmp/g7/RESUME-G7-PHASE2.md into docs/VERSION_TEST_MATRIX_DESIGN.md. On 2026-07-03, Entry 580 found /e/tmp/g7, nc-sweep and phase2-briefs GONE and says 'The in-repo docs are the sole surviving plan - exactly the DEVLOG-579 lesson'. So the plan SURVIVED because the rule had been applied, and this episode is the rule working. What was lost was the oo-plan brief, which had never been folded into the repo. (b) '~362 k tokens for one regenerated brief' is wrong. Entry 584 says the ~362k paid for a 3-scout + 1-writer re-scout (37 findings) that refreshed the whole canonical OO deep-dive, with the brief regenerated inside it. No cost of the brief alone was ever measured. (c) 'A rule that existed only in a transcript was lost' is wrong. Entry 1130 says the rule 'lived only in a transcript' and then moved it into scripts/spec/phase_b_batch.py, so it was at risk, not lost. On battle-testing the record is mixed. phase_b_batch.py was reused across later sessions (DEVLOG:14002, 17704, 25845, 26350). But the same failure came back on 2026-09-23 (Entry 1664: wave 58's practices were live only because a scratchpad survived a reboot). The unenforced rule therefore did not hold for about two months, and held only once check_practices.py enforced it. Scope is also overstated: workstream SKILL.md section 1 deliberately keeps per-run reports and checkpoints in the session scratchpad. The rule actually in force (MANDATORY-PRACTICES header) covers instructions and practices. Missing for VETTED: a correct problem statement, a cost actually attributable to the loss, and the recurrence plus the enforcement that finally made the rule stick.

validator.title: Re-verify a plan's anchors before a multi-wave phase
validator.root_cause: Confirmed by inspection. DEVLOG 870 (2026-07-17): P10's audit 'drifted in five of six re-checked claims'. DEVLOG 923 (2026-07-19): the 9-agent re-scout doc 'duplicated live diagnostic-band state in ~40 places' because 'every wave section independently allocated codes starting from the then-next-free 1570', which collided with each other and with shipped codes 1570-1577. validator.evidence: '~5 of 6' matches DEVLOG.md:37612 and 37633. '~40' is right in magnitude, but the source says ~40 PLACES duplicating live state, with the overlapping claims concentrated in 1570-1574. That is not 40 distinct collisions. Dates 2026-07-17 to 07-19 are correct.
validator.battle_tested: The re-scout half ran repeatedly and paid off each time. P11 ran an 11-scout re-scout before any code (DEVLOG 871, PHASE-11-scout-notes.md). P12 ran a 6-scout plus verify re-scout, and 'the plan drifted in every checked case' (DEVLOG ~37250). The central-allocation half has been in force since 2026-09-23 (MANDATORY-PRACTICES P8). Trains with pre-assigned diagnostic ranges report 'no range collided across clusters' (DEVLOG 6173, 9744, 5995, 7601). Note that the persisted re-scout doc itself went stale (DEVLOG 923), so live state belongs in one place and a re-scout is re-verified at apply time. (a) Figures. Entry 870 (2026-07-17): the P10 audit 'drifted in five of six re-checked claims'. Its corrections were wrong clause numbers, gaps that had already landed, and a mislabel. Those are mostly errors made when the audit was written, not stale reads, so the root cause fits P12 better (Entry 880: a plan written before P8-P11 landed). Entry 923 (2026-07-19): the P13 scout 'duplicated live diagnostic-band state in ~40 places', every wave section allocating from 1570. Since 1570-1577 were already used by shipped codes, '~40 colliding sites' is fair. (b) The problem. The ~40-site drift was produced BY a 9-agent re-scout, done before the phase and saved as a doc. Later saved scout docs also carried errors that needed correction banners (DEVLOG:9126 Wave-H scout; :9640 wave-C scout doc). DEVLOG:20900 (2026-08-09) marks a frozen map 'anchors to be re-scouted at apply'. The skills now in force reject the up-front form: agent-fleet SKILL.md section 2 says 'Don't pre-generate codebase maps with agents instead: they cost a fleet to write and go stale at the next landing', and MANDATORY-PRACTICES P6 requires orientation 'derived on each run, never stale'. No pre-phase re-scout appears in the DEVLOG after 2026-08-09. It was used for about three phases (P11-P13; P12 caught the IEEE-754 inversion) and then replaced. The lesson that survived and is battle-tested is different: check every fact when you use it (agent-fleet section 2 'verified in this session'; P8 cite.py --check), plus central id allocation. Central allocation is well exercised ('no range collided', DEVLOG:6173, 7601, 9744). It still leaked when a second allocator existed (PB939, DEVLOG:5654; PB1537, Entry 1686), and its stated reason in the skill is the 2026-09-02 'five id collisions in one day' (Entry 1430), not the 923 incident.
